Both the changes of α (Fig. 3(a)) and β (Fig. 3(b)) have similar effects on the damping constant χ; as the value of α or β increases, χ decreases, and, therefore, the penetration depth of the laser pulse increases. As the inner area is heated with a larger α or β, the depth of the hole drilled by one pulse increases, as shown in Table 1. These results validated the increase of the model flexibility. As an example, with diferent values of α and β, the results of temperature distribution were diff erent as compared in Fig. 3(c); however, the results of the hole depths can be similar as shown in Table 1. The hole depths were 0.626 m when α = 5.0 and β = 0.01, and 0.680 m when α = 2.0 and β = 1.0.
Table 1. Simulated depth [m] of holes drilled by one laser pulse, with different values of α and β.

The results of the drilling experiment are shown in Fig. 4. The depth of the drilled holes increased as the environmental temperature rose. Here, we considered that the fi nal temperature difference of the material was resulted from the dif erence of initial temperature (environmental temperature). If the initial temperature is higher, there would be more volume of the material reaching the boiling point (criteria of removal) and considered removed, causing the increase of drilling depth. The absorption coefi cient of the material at 25 C and higher temperature (up to 370 C) are not significantly diferent [39]. Therefore, it is appropriate to consider that the material absorbed almost the same energy from the laser irradiation at different environmental temperature (up to 370 C), indicating that the temperature increments of the material should be nearly the same, although the increments could be slightly different due to the different specifi c heat capacity at diferent temperature.
